speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Speaker, I wish to discuss our co-curricular activities (CCA) system.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A resident in my ward shared her son's story with me.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He started playing tennis when he was seven.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: His primary school did not offer tennis as a CCA, so his parents arranged training outside – once a week with a private coach, twice a week in a small group programme.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For six years, he trained largely on his own.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He never had a chance to play alongside peers of his age.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: His dream all through primary school was simple: to join a secondary school with a strong tennis team and finally be part of one.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He applied through Direct School Admission (DSA) to his dream school.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The school took a handful of boys, all top ranked players in their age group.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He worked hard for his Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE) and earned his place on merit.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He made it to the final round but was not selected.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: At this school, trials are conducted before students submit their CCA choices.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The school explained that there was no room, space constraints, grading considerations.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is one of the few CCA with vacancies and open to beginners.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: With that and a heavier Secondary 1 workload, he had to give up competitive tennis.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He can still hit a ball on weekends, but he cannot train seriously.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: His mother told me it was heartbreaking to watch her son give up the sport he loves, not because he was not good enough, but because the system would not give him a chance to become good enough.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Each January, Secondary 1 students submit a ranked list of CCA preferences.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: For popular CCAs, sports, performing arts, schools conduct trials and auditions.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Students who do not pass are asked to remove that CCA from their choices.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Resources are finite, but consider what makes CCA different from everything else in our education system.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Students must participate for four to five years.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Under LEAPS 2.0, that participation is graded and those grades translate into bonus points for post-secondary admission.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We have spent the last decade making the rest of our system more open.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Mid-year exams removed, PSLE T-scores replaced with broader bands, streaming dissolved into subject based banding.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Each reform carries the same signal: less sorting, more room.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: There is a model already operating in Singapore – in our international schools.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: At Singapore American School, students who miss the competitive team are not turned away.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They join a developmental programme and continue training.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is an established system, on Singapore soil, showing that open participation and competitive excellence reinforce each other.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This principle is not foreign to local schools.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Hwa Chong's track and field programme – the first school to win all four divisions at the National Schools Championships in a single year – requires no prior experience and welcomes anyone with a passion for the sport.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It fields athletes across every event category: sprints, jumps, throws, walks, cross-country, pole vault.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A 2008 report on the National Schools Championships observed that while a rival school matched Hwa Chong in first-place finishes, Hwa Chong's depth across the field – finishers in every event accumulating points – was what secured the divisional title.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Broad participation is not the enemy of competitive excellence.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: At Hwa Chong, it is the competitive strategy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Durham University fields 16,000 students across 550 teams, 75% of its student body, and it is the top-ranked team sport university in Britain.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In the United States, eight million high schoolers play athletics; at the college level, over two million play club sport alongside half a million National Collegiate Athletic Association varsity athletes.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The base of the pyramid and the peak are not in competition.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Its Children's Rights in Sport provisions, adopted in 1987, guarantee every child the right to choose whichever sport they choose to participate in.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Selection determines competitive squads, but no child is excluded.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That system, in a country of 5.6 million people, our size, has produced 445 Winter Olympic medals, more than any country on earth.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I also want to turn to DSA, because DSA and CCA are entangled.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When a tennis CCA has 20 spots and half are reserved for DSA students, the remaining places must absorb the entire non-DSA cohort – through trials and leftover places.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That boy in my ward trained for six years and earned his school place on merit.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But the system had already given away half the seats before he arrived.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The question is straightforward: who has access to the preparation that DSA awards?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Competitive sport at age 12 requires years of coaching, tournament entry fees and parents with the time and means to support it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That is not an isolated bad actor – it is a market responding to a system where the stakes are high and the pathways narrow.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Sports science is settling on this question and it is not a close call.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But adult world-class performance is predicted by the opposite pattern: limited early discipline-specific practice, extensive multi-disciplinary engagement and gradual initial progress.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: World-class athletes averaged involvement in two other sports over nine years during childhood.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A companion meta-analysis supported it: the predictors of junior elite success were the precise opposite of the predictors of senior world-class success.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: These advantages typically diminish or reverse by adulthood.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It further recommended that since current performance is a poor predictor of future potential, selection should consider "side-entry" athletes and prioritise those with sustainable development patterns, such as moderate main-sport practice combined with other sports.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It may produce results in the National School Games.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But a system optimised for junior results, by the best available science, is not selecting for true adult world-class performers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: NYSI's Junior Sports Academy exposes Primary 4 to 5 students to four different sports over two years.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: NYSI's Head of Sport Science has stated publicly that broad-based sporting experience produces equal or better outcomes through cross-transfer of skills.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: NYSI even hosted a dialogue with one of the principal authors of that 2025 Science study, Prof Arne Gullich, in 2019, to discuss these principles.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, the gap is not between what we know and what we do not know.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is between what our institutions endorse and what our CCA system requires.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Let us close the gap between rhetoric and reality.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Extend the primary school pilot to secondary schools.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Let trials determine who makes the competitive squad, not who gets to participate.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Every student should be able to join at least one of their top CCA choices.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Where a CCA conducts selection trials, these trials should sort students into a competitive squad and a developmental programme – not into participants and the excluded.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Students in the developmental tier train on fundamentals, fitness and game understanding, with the opportunity to trial for the competitive squad each year.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is how Singapore American School and Hwa Chong already do it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Schools should also survey incoming Secondary 1 students on their CCA preferences and publish the aggregate results.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If 60 students want badminton and a school caps it at 20, that gap should be visible.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Where demand consistently exceeds supply, schools should adjust.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Some may move quickly, splitting sessions or expanding squads within the year.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Others may take two to three years to reallocate resources from persistently under-subscribed CCAs.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What matters is having a credible adjustment mechanism.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And because CCA choices at 13 years old are often made under constraint – a student allocated their third or fourth preference or a student who discovers a genuine passion through a developmental tier – I propose that students be allowed to change CCAs at the end of Secondary 1 or end of Secondary 2 without penalty under LEAPS.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But a programme of this scale serving 232 out of roughly 40,000 Secondary 1 students each year is a proof of concept.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Two, publish a sport-by-sport availability map, showing which sports are offered at which schools, so that gaps are visible and planning is data-driven.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Three, publish a five-year SP-CCA expansion roadmap with clear targets and invite schools to form voluntary geographic clusters of four to six schools, pooling CCA offerings, so students can cross-attend.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If tennis is only available at 30 schools, it should be an SP-CCA candidate.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The boy in my ward, the one who trained for six years, would have had a path.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This also creates natural opportunities for the kind of social mixing across school types that the hon Member David Hoe has spoken about.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We should also recognise sport pursued outside school.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: SportSG already runs ActiveSG Academies and Clubs – affordable, structured programmes in football, basketball, tennis, athletics and other sports, designed for children and youths.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Could students participating in a structured external programme – ActiveSG, a National Sports Association, or a registered academy – be eligible for CCA recognition, subject to verification by the school?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And at primary level, could we double or triple the Junior Sports Academy intake – this fully Ministry of Education (MOE)-funded, non-competitive, multi-sport programme – given demand already exceeds supply?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Third, build the infrastructure to keep these doors open.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If we ask schools to offer a developmental tier alongside competition, we need people to run it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But we should consider whether a lighter certification pathway, suited to teaching fundamentals rather than competitive technique, might widen the coaching pool.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Parent volunteers, older club players, retired coaches, polytechnic and Institute of Technical Education sport graduates who complete coaching practicals but cannot coach in schools without full certification, even full-time National Servicemen with sporting backgrounds could contribute meaningfully at the developmental level if the credentialing framework made room for them.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Norway's 9,500 sports clubs are almost entirely volunteer-run.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Three-quarters of all coaches are unpaid volunteers operating under a tiered credentialing system.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A country our size sustains developmental coaching across every sport because its framework makes room for volunteers, not only professionals.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Holders could lead developmental CCA sessions under periodic supervision by fully certified coaches.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Two further changes are needed to align the system's incentives with its stated developmental purpose.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When bonus points depend on competition results and school representation, schools have a structural incentive to limit CCA places to students who boost competitive outcomes.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When my hon colleague Ms Eileen Chong asked for this data, the Minister said that MOE does not collect it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I would respectfully suggest that this is a question worth answering.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If DSA in sports systematically advantages families who can afford years of private coaching, then it is not a merit pathway.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is a wealth pathway with a merit label.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is a core concern of the Workers' Party that wealth does not compound unfairness or widen social gaps through our education system – points eloquently elaborated over the years by my hon colleagues Mr Gerald Giam and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That resident also has a younger daughter, at a different school.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The girl had never held a badminton racket in her life, but she signed up for badminton because she was curious.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is whether the school opens the door or closes it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He earned his place in a secondary school that was strong in tennis.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And the system told him: there is no room.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He is now in his prime developmental years and he is playing a sport he did not choose, while the sport he loves slips further away with each passing term.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: His mother told me: "I will always wonder whether, if the school had been more open, my son might have improved and eventually earned a place on the team.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is something we will never have the chance to find out." We have an opportunity to make a system that is genuinely open, to extend to CCAs the same generosity of spirit that has guided every other recent reform of our schools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Other Members, like Mr Shawn Huang, Ms Mariam Jaafar, Mr Melvin Yong, Miss Rachel Ong and Mr Gerald Giam have also made similar calls in the past.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: By the way, if you recognise the term "ECA", like me, you are probably of a certain vintage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: We want to nurture our students holistically into people who are intellectually curious, morally grounded, physically active and socially responsible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: It was a simple change of a letter, but it sent a deeper message that CCAs are not "extras" or add-ons, but they are an integral part of our holistic education.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Education must go beyond academics and the confines of the classroom to also foster character, teamwork and resilience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: In this regard, CCAs provide authentic settings where students build character and apply values learned in the classroom – teamwork, resilience, empathy and leadership.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Many of us here will recall our own school experiences or hear stories about this: friendships forged through a uniformed group, perseverance tested on the sports field or creativity sparked in a performing arts ensemble.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: A few years ago, the hockey boys from St Hilda's Secondary School trained hard for their first post-pandemic National School Games competition and they won their opening match.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: But hours later, they would receive crushing news.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Their coach had just passed away sadly from a heart attack.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Their CCA teachers, Glenn and Caleb, would check in on them every day.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Team Captain Nabeel would continually remind them of their coach's belief: "Never stop fighting till the final whistle is blown".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Alumni would take time off work and school to coach and train the boys.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: One of the alumni, Kishon, said "The team needs support now, more than ever.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: How can I abandon them in a time of need?" The team would go on to complete their games.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: As a tribute to their coach, the whole team wore T-shirts under their jerseys that read "For you, Coach Kader".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: I tell this story because CCA is important to us and to our students.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: It enhances their confidence, teamwork skills, communication abilities and a sense of school belonging.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Studies have shown this and these are consistent with global studies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: But these outcomes are only possible because our principals, teachers, parents and students heeded our call in 1999 and made CCAs an integral part of our education.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: I also want to take this moment to thank our educators, parents and Members for their strong support for CCAs so that we can achieve holistic education outcomes for our students.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: In earlier decades, CCAs placed more emphasis on discipline and school identity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Over time, they have also become platforms for nurturing leadership and civic engagement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: It was a deliberate step to focus more on quality over quantity and to reduce the excessive competition to 'chase' down to the last point.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: This reflected the feedback from parents, educators and students who felt that the previous framework had been overly competitive, including some of the other things that the Member has mentioned.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Nevertheless, Mr Speaker, we acknowledge the CCA landscape is not perfect and challenges remain, something that many Members of Parliament have raised over the years, including the ones that the Member has just mentioned.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: On access, and selecting one's favourite CCAs, we are working to further widen access for students to a greater diversity of CCAs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: I had a very serious conversation with the Acting Minister for Culture, Community and Youth about widening this access, but in case you are in doubt, that is also me.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: But that is the benefit of having multiple portfolios.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: We can bring together the strengths of different Ministries to work better for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Members may also be aware of the SP-CCA, the Member mentioned it as well, which enables secondary school students to pursue activities beyond what their individual schools offer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: There is also the multi-school CCA, which is another ground up initiative where schools come together to offer CCAs to students that they could not otherwise have done.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: I will further expand on these efforts, so that students, regardless of school size, have access to quality and diverse CCA experiences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: I will announce more details at the MCCY’s Committee of Supply (COS) debates later.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: I am also glad that the Member agrees with Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh and my discussion this morning about the need to account for potential over early selection, and our improvements and the shifts in DSA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: We will continue to ensure that students from disadvantaged backgrounds are supported.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: Our schools, as the Member has pointed out, already bear the cost of running CCAs, including fees for instructors and equipment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: We will continue to do what we need to do to make sure that students from disadvantaged backgrounds are not deprived of CCA participation because of financial reasons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: CCAs are a part of a much larger educational experience that develops our students to their fullest potential.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: MOE also provides a range of avenues such as the art, music, and physical education curriculum and various Applied Learning Programmes and Learning for Life Programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: The Member also spoke about availability of coaches, and as I am sure he will know, during our debate earlier this year about the Singapore Sports Council (Amendment) Bill that NROC certification is required for the safety of our student.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: And it is something that is very welcome by Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: I think you will have to continue to require that our coaches do possess NROC certification.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: While we have done much, we will continue to improve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: As our Prime Minister has said in his Budget Speech, "Every Singaporean, regardless of where they start in life, should have a fair chance to pursue their aspirations and realize their full potential." I believe this is no different in terms of gaining access to CCA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: It is not possible for me to reply to every single one, but I also want to thank him for recognising the importance of CCAs in our schools.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: CCAs are very much an integral part of our Singapore's education system and one that endeavours to develop every Singaporean into confident citizens.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: They give our students space to discover their passion and to contribute to their communities, and to develop into confident persons and concerned citizens.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education (Mr David Neo)
text: As our society evolves, so must our approach to holistic education.
